claims.text: Stability of equimolar single-phase HEA nanoparticles across 473–1923 K is governed by a threshold balance between mixing enthalpy and atomic-size mismatch.
Moderate mixing enthalpy and low atomic-size mismatch favor maintenance of a solid-solution phase.
High configurational entropy favors the alloy phase, particularly at high temperature.
High configurational entropy produces sluggish atomic diffusion by increasing diffusion barriers.
Sluggish atomic diffusion kinetically stabilizes the nanoparticle solid solution.

Above critical mixing-enthalpy or atomic-size-mismatch values, thermodynamic driving forces overcome kinetic barriers and cause intermetallic formation or phase separation during high-temperature operation.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, single-phase, equimolar solid solutions.
Changing elemental composition while retaining equimolar ratios can systematically tune mixing enthalpy and atomic-size mismatch.
Short-range atomic ordering controls diffusion barriers that mediate kinetic stabilization.
Higher mixing enthalpy or larger atomic-size mismatch lowers kinetic diffusion barriers.
Nanoparticles with moderate mixing enthalpy and minimal atomic-size mismatch will remain homogeneous solid solutions throughout 473–1923 K.

Nanoparticles with increased mixing enthalpy or size mismatch will exhibit elemental segregation, distinct domains, phase separation, or intermetallic formation at the upper end of the temperature range.
An optimized multielement nanoparticle baseline can remain uniformly dispersed and chemically homogeneous up to 873 K.
The critical stability thresholds may depend on particle size, synthesis conditions, and the specific elemental combination.
Exact critical values of mixing enthalpy and atomic-size mismatch are not specified.
Failure of high-enthalpy or high-mismatch nanoparticles to transform, or degradation of the optimized comparison nanoparticles, would falsify the proposed threshold relationship.
